benchmarks.name: YourMechanic (BMW 328i xDrive 2.0T)
benchmarks.note: 2013-2016 2.0L turbo estimates; page quotes shop/dealer prices of $1,762-$2,746; the same page's headline 'average $464' conflicts with its own table

finding: The live range of $270-$975 starts too low and stops slightly short. Implied totals (parts + hours x $120-$160/hr): midsize 2016 Camry about $341-$863 (1.0 hr, from a shop's stated book time for a 2007 4-cylinder Camry); truck 2016 F-150 5.0L about $481-$987 (2.0 hr, a parts seller's install estimate, not a book time). Economy (2015 Corolla) and luxury (2015 BMW 328i) totals could not be computed because no stated labor time was found for those vehicles; their parts alone run $233-$551 and $360-$460 (the BMW figure is remanufactured OEM-brand only; no genuine BMW list price was found). The cheapest remanufactured alternator we found for any of the four vehicles was $221 before any labor, so a $270 total is not realistic for a shop job; our lowest implied total is $341, and RepairPal's lowest per-model figure is $527. At the top, $975 roughly covers a mainstream truck with a list-price OEM part ($987) but sits below RepairPal's national high of $1,088 and far below estimates for European cars (about $1,440 for a 328i 2.0T at YourMechanic). On our own evidence a range of roughly $340-$990 fits mainstream vehicles, with a note that luxury/European and hard-to-reach alternators run well above it. Only Jerry's '$259-$491' headline supports the current low end, and Jerry's own table contradicts it.
extras: Quotes often add: charging-system diagnosis or battery/alternator test fee, a new serpentine belt and sometimes tensioner, a new battery if the old one was damaged by under- or over-charging, a refundable core charge on remanufactured units, battery registration/coding on some European cars, shop supplies, and sales tax.
